issues:
The checker's verdict holds, and both of its confirmed citations survive my own fetch.

Morwani et al. 2311.07568v2, Lemma 6, verbatim: "all points in the support of q* are on the margin for any maximum margin solution". The closer dense analogue of "hardest wrong answers" is condition C.1 together with App. F.2: "for each input (a,b), f takes the same value on all incorrect labels c'". In the dense case all p-1 wrong answers tie; in ours at least 2K do.

Shapley-Snow: Crossref for DOI 10.1515/9781400881727-004 gives 1951 and pp. 27-36. The bib entry's 1950 and 27-35 match common usage, including the citation in Attia and Oliu-Barton, but not the DOI record. This is minor. The statement is confirmed through Attia and Oliu-Barton 1810.08798v2: Thm 2.3.1, and Prop 2.3.4(iii) for uniqueness.

Prior art the checker missed. These are ML and optimisation analogues of the mechanism, not of the result:
(1) Breiman 1999, Neural Computation. Def 2.2 casts minimum-margin maximisation over convex combinations of base predictors as a zero-sum matrix game. Our s=1 programme is exactly this game, with frequencies as base predictors and offsets as instances. It is the ML-native bridge to Shapley-Snow.
(2) Ge, Jiang and Ye 2011, Math. Programming, Thm 3: the local minimisers of sum x_j^p (0<p<1) over {Ax=b, x>=0} are exactly the basic feasible solutions. This is the l_p form of the "concave budget forces a vertex" step, with r=1/s<1. It assumes a bounded feasible set, and P_p is unbounded, so cite it with "cf.".
(3) Rosset, Zhu and Hastie 2004, JMLR. The l1-margin/boosting solution has at most n nonzero coefficients, and the nonzeros solve "|A| equations in |A| variables".

I ran an adversarial arXiv sweep over about 60 recent modular-addition papers (to 2609.26679) and read the closest margin-theory ones: 2511.23443, 2506.06489, 2608.04451, 2606.05863, He et al. 2602.16849/2606.02993, Tian 2410.01779 and Li et al. 2402.09469. None has K tight offsets, an equalising system, vertices or Shapley-Snow.

Wording caveat for the recommended sentence: at s=1 a maximiser need not be a vertex. The Shapley-Snow link holds only for extreme (basic) optimal strategies, so say that explicitly.

extra_citations.why: Casts maximising the minimum margin of a convex combination of base predictors as a zero-sum matrix game (Def 2.2, minimax value). At s=1 our programme is exactly this game, with frequencies as predictors and offsets as instances. This gives the ML-native framing for invoking Shapley-Snow in the bottleneck remark. Metadata is from Crossref.

Thm 3: basic feasible solutions are exactly the local minimisers of sum x_j^p (0<p<1) over {Ax=b, x>=0}. This is the l_p analogue of the step that the concave budget sum v_j^{1/s} forces a vertex, which yields the full-rank active set. The theorem assumes a bounded feasible set, so cite it with "cf." (P_p is unbounded). Metadata is from Crossref.

Optional. Classic ML statement that the l1-margin maximiser has at most n nonzero coefficients, with the nonzeros fixed by |A| equations in |A| unknowns (Sec 5.1.1, App B Thm 3). It is the ML form of "#features bounded by #binding constraints, square system"; our proposition is the per-constraint refinement of it.
